tagline: Desert water knowledge shaped a stage road toward the Colorado River.
intro: The Bradshaw Trail crosses desert country on a 70-mile dirt road that Riverside County periodically grades. Soft sand interrupts the route, which runs mostly across public land. BLM’s Back Country Byway offers views of the Chuckwalla Bench and the Orocopia, Chuckwalla and Mule Mountains. The surviving California portion received its byway designation in 1992.

The route belonged to an Indigenous trade network before William Bradshaw established his stage road in 1862. Cabazon, a Cahuilla chief, and a visiting Maricopa shared knowledge of the route’s springs and water holes with Bradshaw. The stage route carried miners and other passengers toward the La Paz gold fields from 1862 to 1877. That historical journey began in San Bernardino, far beyond the surviving recreational road’s western end. County maps later called the road the Butterfield Trail; in June 1974, Riverside County’s supervisors restored the Bradshaw name, before its recognition as a backcountry byway.

Traveling west to east, the route begins near Dos Palmas, with the Orocopia Mountains at the western end of the mountain sequence. The Chuckwalla Mountains lie north of the trail, followed farther east by the Mule Mountains and the Palo Verde Valley. Near Ripley, the eastern end meets 30th Avenue west of State Route 78.

moments.title: Orocopia Mountains
moments.text: The historical Bradshaw Trail passed through the Orocopia Mountains’ southeastern foothills. Water helped define that journey: Bradshaw traveled to Bitter Spring at the foothills, then continued to the existing stage stop at Dos Palmas Spring. From Dos Palmas, his party took a pass between the Orocopia and Chocolate ranges. The Orocopias lie east of the Coachella Valley and north of the Salton Sea. BLM manages the Orocopia Mountains Wilderness, where remnant spring-fed oases support California fan palms. Movement along the adjacent San Andreas Fault helped shape the range’s varied terrain over thousands of years.

moments.title: Chuckwalla Mountains
moments.text: The Chuckwalla Mountains border the trail on its northern side, with steep-walled canyons, washes and isolated rock outcrops within the range. Bradshaw’s party skirted the southern end, using a route whose water holes included Chuckwalla Springs. The mountains take their name from chuckwalla lizards. On their southern flank, the Chuckwalla Bench is an Area of Critical Environmental Concern frequented by desert tortoises. BLM designated most of the mountains as wilderness in 1994. Ocotillo, cholla, yucca and creosote grow in this Colorado Desert range, separated from the Little Chuckwalla Range by Graham Pass.

moments.title: Mule Mountains
moments.text: A gap in the Mule Mountains brought Bradshaw’s party into the Palo Verde Valley. The range stands west of the valley and the Colorado River, marking the eastern part of this desert crossing. Mule Spring was one of the water holes along the historical route. Beyond the mountains, the party crossed the valley to Bradshaw’s Ferry, then continued upstream toward the gold fields of La Paz. The present trail ends near Ripley at 30th Avenue, west of State Route 78. The mountains run northeast to southwest, crossing the county line from Riverside into Imperial County.

practical: Orocopia Mountains: BLM reports flash-flood impacts on routes in the Bradshaw Trail area and recommends four-wheel drive for soft sand. Check weather before traveling. There are no amenities on the trail. The posted Chocolate Mountain Aerial Gunnery Range borders part of the trail to the south and is a live bombing range. (checked 2026-10-11)
